subtitle: "marrow compile — the AOT lane, exposed to users"

Everything else in this guide runs through the Python bindings: build a plan,
call `.execute()`, get a `RecordBatch` back, in the same process that built
the plan. `marrow compile` is a different thing entirely — it turns a Mojo
source file into a standalone binary that runs the query later, from the
command line, with no marrow, no Mojo toolchain and no Python interpreter
installed on the machine that runs it.

::: {.callout-note}
The code on this page is Mojo, compiled ahead of time — not the Python
`marrow.expr` API the rest of this guide uses. See
[Expression execution](expressions.qmd) for the lazy Python frontend.
:::

## When to reach for this instead of the lazy frontend

The query *shape* — which relation nodes, in what order, over which columns
— is frozen at compile time. Only **scalars and paths** are late-bound,
through a new `param()` node that sits alongside `col()` and `lit()`. That is
the whole trade:

- A fixed report that runs against a different file and a different
  threshold every day — `marrow compile` fits well. Ship one binary, run it
  with different `--flag` values, no marrow install required on the target
  machine.
- A query whose *shape* varies — a different filter, a different set of
  group-by keys, an ad hoc notebook session — wants the
  [Python lazy frontend](expressions.qmd) instead. Reshaping a plan there is
  a line of Python; reshaping a compiled binary is a rebuild.

**State the cost up front, because it will not announce itself:** a
`marrow compile` build takes roughly **1-2 minutes per invocation**, because
`mojo build` elaborates the whole of `marrow` at `-O3` for every compile —
there is no incremental build. That is fine for a binary you build once and
run many times; it is a bad fit for an edit-compile-run loop.

## `param()` — the late-bound value

`param(name, dtype)` returns an expression node structurally identical to
`lit(value)`, except the scalar behind it lives in a cell that starts unbound
and is filled in from the command line after the plan is built. It composes
with everything a literal does — comparisons, arithmetic, a `ParquetScan`
path — and it costs nothing extra per row: the cell is resolved once per
batch, not once per element.

```mojo
from marrow.expr.builders import col, param
from marrow.dtypes import int64, string

var src   = param("src", string)              # required, no default
var min_a = param("min-a", int64, default=0)   # optional, falls back to 0
```

`param()` is overloaded for numeric, string and temporal dtypes in the fused
(AOT) lane, and there is a runtime-lane counterpart,
`param(name, dtype, default=..., help=...)`, at parity with it — a compiled
query is free to mix `param()` cells with plain `col()`/`lit()` expressions
and runtime-typed (`DynValue`) ones in the same plan.

**One name is one parameter.** Mentioning the same name twice — in both lanes,
or twice in one — does not make two parameters: the second `param("min-a", …)`
shares the cell the first one created, so the single `--min-a` flag binds
every mention of it. Redeclaring a name with a *different* dtype is an error;
`default` and `help` are taken from the first declaration, so write them at
the first mention.

A temporal parameter is spelled on the command line as its epoch integer in
the dtype's own unit — the same spelling `default=` takes:

```bash
$ ./q --cutoff 1560601845     # param("cutoff", timestamp(second))
```

A `ParquetScan`'s `path` accepts a `param()` cell directly in place of a
literal string, so the file a compiled binary reads is late-bound too, not
just the predicate thresholds:

```mojo
ParquetScan[...](path=param("src", string), schema=sch)
```

## `plan.execute_cli()` — the compiled binary's entry point

The last call in `main()`, once the plan is built, is `plan.execute_cli()`
instead of `print(plan.execute())`. It:

1. drains every `param()` declaration the plan's construction registered,
2. checks `argv` for `--help` or `--describe` and short-circuits to a
   rendered summary before binding or running anything — a `--help` run
   never needs dummy values for the plan's parameters,
3. otherwise binds each declared parameter from `--name value` pairs (or
   applies its declared default), raising a named error for a missing
   required parameter or an unrecognized flag,
4. executes the plan, and
5. writes the result: to stdout by default, or to a file when `-o` is given.

## The runnable example

The file below is `benchmarks/binary_size/query_param.mojo` in the repo — the
same file `pixi run binary_size query_param query_scan_typed` compiles to
measure what a late-bound parameter costs in `__text`. It is embedded here
with Quarto's `include` shortcode rather than copied, so this page is
byte-identical to the source file and cannot silently drift out of sync with
it the way a pasted-in snippet could.

It is **not executed by the docs build** — a `mojo build` here takes 1-2
minutes and the `docs` pixi environment carries no Mojo toolchain, so
running it as part of `pixi run -e docs docs` is not practical. What follows
is instead the exact transcript of compiling and running this file, captured
by hand while writing this page:

```{.mojo filename="benchmarks/binary_size/query_param.mojo"}
{{< include ../../benchmarks/binary_size/query_param.mojo >}}
```

```bash
$ marrow compile benchmarks/binary_size/query_param.mojo -o q
$ ./q --help
Parameters:
  --src <string> (required)
  --min-a <int64> (required)
$ ./q --src data.parquet --min-a 5
RecordBatch(num_rows=2, schema=Schema(fields=[a: int64]))
$ ./q --src data.parquet --min-a 5 -o result.parquet
```

`data.parquet` above was a five-row file with an `int64` column `a` holding
`[1, 5, 10, 2, 7]`; `--min-a 5` keeps the two rows greater than 5 (`10` and
`7`), matching the `RecordBatch(num_rows=2, ...)` above, and `result.parquet`
reads back as exactly those two values.

## `marrow compile` — building the binary

Installing marrow with the `compile` extra (`pip install marrow[compile]`)
registers a `marrow` console script backed by `python/marrow/compile.py`.
`compile` is a subcommand of it, so more subcommands can join it later
without another redesign:

```bash
$ marrow compile query.mojo -o query
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The `compile` extra does not resolve on PyPI today

The extra pins `mojo>=1.1,<2`, and marrow needs a **nightly** Mojo build;
PyPI's stable `mojo` package tops out at 1.0.0, so `pip install
marrow[compile]` cannot satisfy it from PyPI alone. Install the nightly
explicitly first — `pip install --pre mojo --extra-index-url
https://whl.modular.com/nightly/simple/` — or work inside marrow's own pixi
environment, which already has the pinned nightly (`pixi run -e dev mojo
build ...`). `check_mojo_version` reports the same thing at run time if the
stable wheel is what got installed.
:::

`marrow` resolves the `mojo` compiler on `PATH` (raising a named error,
including the nightly-vs-stable-PyPI distinction, if it is missing or out of
range) and the `marrow/` Mojo package to pass as `mojo build`'s `-I` — via
`--marrow-path`, the `MARROW_MOJO_PATH` environment variable, the copy
bundled into the wheel, or by walking up from the current directory looking
for a `marrow/` + `pixi.toml` pair, in that order. Then it runs the same
recipe `benchmarks/binary_size/compare.py` uses to build the gate binaries —
`mojo build -O3 -g0 -I <marrow> <src> -o <out>`, then `strip` — so a compiled
query's size is directly comparable to the numbers in
`benchmarks/binary_size/`.

Useful flags:

- **`-o OUTPUT`** (or the positional form, `marrow compile query.mojo out`)
  — where to write the binary. Defaults to the source file's name without
  `.mojo`, in the current directory.
- **`--fast`** — build with `-O1` instead of `-O3`: a faster compile, a
  slower binary. Still on the order of a minute, since elaborating `marrow`
  dominates either way.
- **`--no-writers`** — see below.
- **`--bundle DIR`** — see below.
- **`--marrow-path`, `-v`, `--no-strip`** — override package resolution,
  print the underlying `mojo build` command, or skip stripping debug
  symbols.

### `-o` at run time: writing Parquet or Arrow IPC output

The compiled binary's own `-o` flag (not `marrow compile`'s) picks an output
writer by extension: `-o result.parquet` writes Parquet, `-o result.arrow`
writes Arrow IPC, and `--format parquet|ipc|table` overrides the guess. With
no `-o`, the result prints to stdout as a `RecordBatch`, same as
`print(plan.execute())` in every other example in this guide.

Linking those two writers into the binary is not free: the binary-size gate
measured **572,288 bytes** of `__text` for Parquet + Arrow IPC output, against
a `query_scan_typed` baseline of 2,025,432 bytes:

| Build | `__text` | Delta vs. baseline |
|---|---|---|
| `query_scan_typed` (no `param()`, no `execute_cli()`) | 2,025,432 | — |
| `query_param`, writers gated out (`--no-writers`) | 2,222,132 | +196,700 |
| `query_param`, writers linked (the default) | 2,794,420 | +768,988 |

`marrow compile` passes `-D MARROW_CLI_WRITERS=true` **by default**, so the
documented `-o result.parquet` contract works out of the box. Pass
`--no-writers` for the smaller binary if the query only ever needs to print
or write to a pipe — a `-o result.parquet` against a `--no-writers` build
raises a named error rather than silently doing nothing.

### `--bundle` — a relocatable, self-contained directory

A compiled binary still dynamically links a handful of Mojo/MAX runtime
`.dylib`/`.so` files, resolved through the local pixi environment's rpath —
copying the bare binary to another machine will not run there.
`marrow compile query.mojo -o query --bundle DIR` copies the binary plus the
**transitive** closure of its non-system shared-library dependencies into
`DIR` and
rewrites the rpath to `@loader_path` (macOS) / `$ORIGIN` (Linux), so `DIR`
runs standalone — no pixi environment, no marrow install, on the build
machine or any other with a compatible OS/arch:

```bash
$ marrow compile query.mojo -o query --bundle ./dist
$ ./dist/query --src data.parquet --min-a 5
```

Measured on `query_param`: 4 runtime dylibs (2 linked directly, 2 pulled in
transitively), stripped binary plus dylibs together, **5.5 MB total**. The
closure walks `otool -L` / `ldd` recursively rather than hardcoding a dylib
list, because the set is not fixed — a `-D MARROW_GPU=true` build pulls in
an additional GPU runtime library that a CPU-only build does not link.

**The bundle also includes marrow's Parquet compression codecs** — zstd,
snappy, lz4, zlib and brotli. Those are `dlopen`-ed at runtime rather than
linked (see `marrow/utils/compression.mojo`), so they are invisible to
`otool -L`/`ldd` and need their own step: `--bundle` resolves the active
pixi/conda environment's `lib/` directory (`$CONDA_PREFIX`, or two
directories up from `mojo` on `PATH` — never a hardcoded pixi path) and
copies whichever of the five it finds there, plus their own transitive
dependencies (`libbrotlienc`/`libbrotlidec` each pull in
`libbrotlicommon`). A codec that is not installed in the environment is
skipped with a warning rather than failing the bundle. This matters because
snappy is pyarrow's default Parquet compression — without it, the bundle
could only read uncompressed files. `compression.mojo` tries an
executable-relative path before the bare soname it otherwise `dlopen`s, which
is what makes the staged copy actually get found at runtime; copying alone
is not enough, since a bare `dlopen("libsnappy.dylib")` never searches
`@loader_path`.

Measured on `query_param` with every codec present: **8.8 MB total**
(the codec libraries and their `libc++` dependency add roughly 3.3 MB over
the runtime-only 5.5 MB above; same-content version aliases, e.g.
`libzstd.dylib` and `libzstd.1.dylib`, are written once and symlinked rather
than duplicated).

**Zipping the bundle: use `zip -ry`, not `zip -r`.** A plain `zip -r`
dereferences symlinks, turning each deduplicated alias back into a full copy
of the same bytes — the archive would carry the codec libraries' size twice
over, and the 8.8 MB figure above would not survive the round trip.
`zip -ry DIR.zip DIR` (the `-y` stores symlinks as symlinks) preserves the
dedup; unzip on a machine of the same OS/arch to get the directory back
exactly as built.

**What "self-contained" has and has not been verified to mean.** The bundle's
own binary has its rpath rewritten to `@loader_path`, and that path has been
verified end to end: a snappy-compressed Parquet file reads correctly from a
freshly built bundle run with no `DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH` or `CONDA_PREFIX` set,
from a different working directory, via both a relative (`./query`) and an
absolute-path invocation. What is **not** rewritten is the codec libraries'
*own* `@rpath` entries — `bundle()` only rewrites the main binary's rpath, the
same as it already did for the linked runtime-dylib closure before this
change. In practice that means a codec with its own dependency (`libbrotlienc`
depends on `libbrotlicommon`, for instance) resolves that dependency via the
codec library's rpath as recorded on the *build* machine, which is not
verified to carry over to a different machine. This mirrors the existing,
unfixed behavior for the runtime-dylib closure, so it is not a new gap — full
cross-machine portability of every codec remains an open question, not a
claim this page makes.

Static linking is not on the table for this on macOS — there is no
`libSystem.a` to link against. It may be possible on Linux, where static
linking is at least conceivable; that is untested here (no Linux development
machine at hand) and is one of the open questions this feature shipped with,
not a claim this page makes.
